name: action-domain-responder
intent: Define one server-side request/response transaction as a small Action that extracts transport input, a transport-independent Domain entry point (often a transaction script, service layer or application service), and a Responder that turns the domain result into the response; keep routing and cross-cutting dispatch outside the trio so each role can evolve and be tested independently.
problem: A page/controller method that receives an HTTP request, validates and applies business rules, reads storage and renders a response becomes a fat action: the same input and domain work are hard to reuse from a CLI or message endpoint, representation changes add branches, and tests need the web stack. The failure is not routing itself; it is mixing transport translation, domain decisions and response presentation in one request unit.
context: Server-side request/response boundaries - primarily HTTP, and sometimes a non-interactive CLI, RPC call or request/reply message - where a router or Front Controller can dispatch one method/path to one handler, the Domain must be callable without transport types, and the response may have multiple representations. ADR refines the per-request handler; it does not replace routing, middleware, a Front Controller or the Domain Model, and it is not for client-side UI, streaming or long-lived conversations.
benefits: One action per request keeps each handler small and its dependencies explicit (constructor or parameter injection) instead of a controller class that gains a method, and often shared state, per endpoint.
The Domain stays free of transport types: the same entry point can serve an HTTP action, a CLI command or a queue consumer, and it can be tested without starting a web stack.
Presentation is isolated in a responder, so one action can feed several formats (HTML, JSON, XML, CSV) and content negotiation lives in one place per format.
Action and Responder are separately testable: the action against a stub domain and a stub responder, the responder against a fixed domain payload with no request and no business logic at all.
Adding or changing an endpoint touches one file rather than extending a shared controller, which keeps ownership clear and lets teams work in parallel (open/closed at endpoint granularity).
The uniform one-handler-per-request unit maps cleanly onto route-to-class registries, DI containers and per-endpoint middleware (auth, validation, caching), so dispatch stays declarative.
tradeoffs: Class proliferation: a controller with five action methods can become five Action classes and five Responder classes, with more files, more DI wiring and more navigation (the canonical tradeoff admitted by the pattern's author).

The separation is unenforced discipline: one conditional, loop, try/catch or validation in the Action - or one storage access in the Responder - collapses the roles back into a thin controller, and no compiler stops it.

Cross-cutting concerns must move outside the handler (middleware, filters, interceptors, ActionBuilder), so part of a request's behaviour is no longer visible where the request is handled, which complicates reading and debugging.

The responder indirection costs more than it returns for trivial endpoints: fetching a row and encoding it as JSON does not need three objects, and the pay-off only appears when an endpoint grows a second representation or a second consumer.

Content negotiation happens in the responder, i.e. after the domain has already done its work; an unsatisfiable Accept header therefore needs an early acceptability check in the web handler to avoid wasted work.

Domain-boundary drift: a mechanical reading of 'if it touches storage it belongs to the Domain' pulls sessions, cookies and status-code decisions into business logic, where they are harder to see and test.

participants.responsibility: Receives the HTTP request, routes it to the action registered for that method and path, invokes it, and sends the response the action returns; may pre-check acceptability and applies route-level middleware.

The logic for exactly one request: collects the inputs the domain needs from the request (with defaults, but without business branches), invokes the domain, hands the domain result to the responder and returns the response.

Entry point into the application's business logic (transaction script, service layer, application service or interactor). Receives plain values or a DTO - never the request - and owns validation, persistence, authorization, sessions and error reporting.

Builds the HTTP response from what the action gives it: status code, headers, cookies, content negotiation, formatting and transformation, templates and views. Holds presentation logic only, and no domain access.

Optional value object the domain returns and the responder consumes: the result data plus status or error information, so the action can stay branch-free and the responder can map outcomes to representations.

use_cases: HTTP APIs and REST/JSON endpoints where every route needs its own input collection, its own domain call and its own response shape.

Server-rendered applications where each page or form submission is handled by its own action and rendered by a responder that owns the template (a Template View or Two-Step View lives inside the responder).
Applications that must serve the same domain result in several representations - HTML for browsers, JSON for clients, HAL or CSV for integrations - as one action with one responder per format.
Systems with many small endpoints and several teams, where one class per endpoint removes merge conflicts in shared controllers and makes ownership obvious.
Request/response boundaries beyond HTTP (CLI commands, RPC endpoints, message consumers that answer) where the same domain must be reachable from a second interface without duplicating logic.
Ruby Hanami applications that map each route to an individual action class, keeping the domain service callable without Hanami's request/response objects.
Rails controller actions, Django function-based views, Sinatra route blocks or Express handlers that stay thin and delegate to a transport-neutral service while returning framework response objects.
Play Framework Actions or http4s HttpRoutes that use typed domain results and separate response builders when the same operation serves JSON and HTML.

PHP Aura framework applications that follow the framework guide's ADR recipe: the web handler dispatches to an Action class, the Action calls a Domain service, and a per-action Responder extending a shared AbstractResponder renders the response.

Mezzio (formerly Laminas Expressive) and other PSR-15 pipelines where the innermost RequestHandler consumes a ServerRequestInterface and returns a ResponseInterface, giving the Action-Domain-Responder trio a standardized transport boundary.
avoid_when: A small application, prototype or script: a single framework handler function that calls the domain and writes the response is simpler and loses nothing.

The framework already separates the phases in a way the team is happy with (Rails controllers plus views, Spring MVC plus message converters, NestJS plus interceptors) - adding ADR on top creates classes without removing any.
The interface is not request/response: client-side UIs, streaming pipelines and long-lived sessions are better served by MVC/MVP, pipelines or state machines.
The response is a pure function of the request with no domain involvement (health checks, static proxying, redirects): one handler suffices and a responder is ceremony.
The domain is trivial CRUD with exactly one output format and no second consumer on the horizon - the indirection only pays off when one of those changes.

A microservice mesh where each service boundary is already an ADR endpoint: chaining multiple ADR services over the network multiplies latency and couples services at the network level rather than the domain level.
A Page Controller is already the intended one-object-per-page/request unit and the endpoint is small; adding separate Action and Responder classes only renames the same code without buying reuse.
The concern is dispatch, authentication gates or behavior common to every route: use a Front Controller, router or middleware for that cross-cutting work, then let ADR handle the selected request.

The business rules are a rich object model with invariants and behavior; do not force them into a transaction-script-shaped Domain merely to satisfy ADR - keep a Domain Model behind the Domain entry point.
anti_patterns: Fat action: the Action validates input, branches on business rules, queries storage and formats the body; it is a controller method renamed, so move those responsibilities to the Domain and Responder.
Storage-aware Responder: the Responder fetches widgets, translations or counters; presentation then owns hidden business dependencies, so return the needed data in the Domain Payload.
Method-switched resource Action: one Action branches on request.method; it is a Page Controller with extra dispatch hidden inside, so register one Action per route.
Transport-aware Domain entry point: the Domain accepts an HTTP request, session object or framework type; CLI and message callers now need the web stack, so accept plain values or a DTO.
Configurable mega-Action: one callable triple drives every route; it buys indirection with unreadable wiring, so reserve it for framework infrastructure rather than application code.
Deferred Responder return: the Action returns a Responder for somebody else to invoke; the caller must understand presentation lifecycle, so invoke it inside the Action and return the response.
design_principles: Single responsibility per role: input collection, business logic and presentation are three jobs, held by three collaborators.
Separation of concerns: the HTTP boundary is a thin translation layer over a domain that never learns about it.
Dependency inversion: the action depends on domain and responder abstractions supplied to it, not on concrete infrastructure it constructs.
Open/closed at endpoint granularity: new endpoints and new representations are added as new classes or functions, not as edits to a shared controller.
Dispatch unit equals change unit: one request, one handler, one response keeps the blast radius of a change to one file.
Return the response, not the responder: the action invokes the responder internally and returns the built response to the router, never exposing the responder to the caller.
best_practices: Keep the action conditional-free: collect input with ternaries and defaults, call the domain, call the responder; move every branch into the domain (business) or the responder (format).
Pass plain values or a DTO to the domain, never the request object, and let the domain validate and report failures in a payload the responder can interpret.
Put content negotiation in the responder, but let the router check acceptability first so an unserviceable Accept header fails before the domain runs.
Keep responders format-specific and free of domain access; one responder per (action, format) or one shared responder when the whole interface uses a single format.
Keep authentication and authorization in the domain (they touch storage) and limit the router to anonymity or route-level checks.
Handle domain exceptions in the domain and return status/error information in the payload, so the action never needs a rescue or catch block.
Test the roles separately: the action with stub domain and stub responder, the domain with no HTTP at all, the responder against a fixed payload.
sources: Jones, Paul M., Action Domain Responder (2014) - components, collaborations and the ADR-vs-Model-2 comparison. https://paul-m-jones.com/adr/
https://github.com/pmjones/adr/blob/master/ADR.md
https://github.com/pmjones/adr/blob/master/IMPLEMENTATION.md
https://github.com/pmjones/adr/blob/master/TRADEOFFS.md
Fowler, Martin, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Page Controller, the controller style ADR replaces for single-request endpoints.

Martin Fowler, Transaction Script (2003) - a procedure organizes the logic for one presentation request, making it a possible Domain implementation for ADR. https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/transactionScript.html
Martin Fowler, Page Controller (2003) - one controller handles one page or action; ADR makes the input/domain/output split explicit. https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/pageController.html
Martin Fowler, Front Controller (2003) - centralizes shared request handling and dispatch; it surrounds rather than replaces ADR. https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/frontController.html
Ruby on Rails Guides, Action Controller Overview - routing selects a controller action that processes the request and generates output. https://guides.rubyonrails.org/action_controller_overview.html
Django documentation, Writing views - a view function receives an HttpRequest and returns an HttpResponse. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/http/views/
Sinatra README - each method/path route has a block whose return value becomes the response. https://sinatrarb.com/intro.html
Express.js Routing guide - route methods invoke callback handlers matching the request method and path. https://expressjs.com/en/guide/routing/

Martin Fowler, Anemic Domain Model (2003) - warns against moving all domain behavior into procedural services; use a richer Domain Model when the rules warrant it. https://martinfowler.com/bliki/AnemicDomainModel.html

Paul M. Jones, ADR objections - explains why Front Controller is outside ADR and why ADR is a server-side request/response pattern rather than client-side MVC. https://github.com/pmjones/adr/blob/master/OBJECTIONS.md

Aura for PHP Framework Guide, Action Domain Responder - a framework manual wiring an Action, a Domain service and a per-action Responder via dependency injection. https://auraphp.com/framework/2.x/en/adr/
hanami-action README - Hanami's endpoint component: each action is a single-purpose, Rack-compatible object exposing call(env) and handle(request, response). https://github.com/hanami/hanami-action

PHP-FIG, PSR-15 HTTP Server Request Handlers - the standard for the innermost handler that consumes a ServerRequestInterface and produces a ResponseInterface without delegating. https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-15/

Paul M. Jones, Action Injection as a Code Smell (2017) - controllers accumulating dependencies used by only some actions, the motivation for one Action class per endpoint. https://www.paul-m-jones.com/post/2017-05-16/action-injection-as-a-code-smell/

Paul M. Jones, Solving the Widget Problem in ADR (2017) - page chrome and multi-panel data belong in the Domain payload, not in responder-side fetches. https://paul-m-jones.com/post/2017-12-28/solving-the-widget-problem-in-adr/

Matthew Weier O'Phinney, Better Understanding Controllers Through Basic Patterns (2014) - reads the controller or action as a facade over argument marshalling, domain invocation and response marshalling, framing ADR as a heuristic rather than a prescription. https://mwop.net/blog/2014-06-09-controllers-as-facades.html

related_patterns_notes.page-controller: handles one page or action in one controller; ADR splits that per-request unit into Action, Domain and Responder.
related_patterns_notes.front-controller: centralizes routing and cross-cutting request handling; ADR begins after dispatch at the selected per-request Action.
related_patterns_notes.application-controller: coordinates navigation or workflow across several screens or actions; ADR is the one-request boundary, not the workflow coordinator.
related_patterns_notes.service-to-worker: hands work from a service to a worker for asynchronous execution; ADR is synchronous request/response decomposition unless the Domain explicitly enqueues work.
related_patterns_notes.command: encapsulates an operation and its input, often for a bus or undo; an ADR Action is transport-facing and may invoke a command in its Domain but is not the command itself.
related_patterns_notes.transaction-script: organizes one business transaction as a procedure; it is a valid Domain implementation inside ADR, while ADR also isolates input and response presentation.
related_patterns_notes.application-service: exposes an application use case behind a stable entry point; ADR's Domain role may be an application service, but ADR additionally defines Action and Responder.
related_patterns_notes.template-view: renders a template from supplied data; it may be used inside an ADR Responder, which also sets HTTP status, headers and cookies.
